newsitem.title: GREECE: U.S. warns Greece over intellectual property rights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns Greece over intellectual property rights.

text.p: The United States told Greece Thursday that it was considering trade sanctions to stop violation of intellectual property rights by dozens of small television stations broadcasting American movies without paying royalties.

"It (sanctions) is certainly an option," U.S. Deputy Assistant Trade Representative Joe Papovich told a news conference. "I will report back in Washington and a decision will be taken around the middle of December."
Papovich said Greece had made no progress in curbing piracy in the past two years and that in 1995 U.S. companies had lost $102 million from violation of property rights.
Piracy in motion pictures made up $60 million in losses and the remainder came from sound recordings, computer programmes, business software and entertainment software.
Greece passed a media law in 1995 protecting intellectual property rights but Papovich said it was not being enforced.

"We want the government to enforce the copyright law which is not being enforced. We want action not words because the U.S. considers intellectual stealing the same as physical stealing. We want royalties to be paid."
Greece is on Washington's "priority watch list," which does not call for the implementation of trade sanctions.
However, depending on Papovich's proposals after meetings with government officials, it could be moved up to the "priority foreign country" list, where sanctions are an option.
Trade sanctions for violating copyright laws will primarily result to an increase of tariffs on Greek exports to the United States.
"I can't comment on what I will propose or what Washington may decide," Papovich said. "I still have a number of meetings with Greek government officials."
